title: v5 verdict: grounded+retrieved knowledge made ON do 29% MORE work — task wasn't hard enough to need it. The win-regime is narrow.
summary: v5-grounded (n=5 opus, 10/10 solved) tested the closed loop: ingested KB → search_knowledge retrieval → measure. Retrieval WORKED (every ON arm called search_knowledge 1×, engaged the anchor note 'cross-session IDs must be namespaced' 5-7× per transcript). But RESULT: H_on=2,674 > H_off=2,023 — ON did 1.29× MORE output/work, plus C=18,329 consult overhead → METRIC −21,582 → NO-WIN. WHY (the flipped failure mode): the v5 task's hardness was LOW (H_off ~2k vs v4's ~18k) — OFF solved it easily without the note. So the grounded knowledge had little hardness to collapse, and the ON arm RETRIEVING + REASONING ABOUT whether/how to apply the note was pure overhead — it over-engaged (more cautious/thorough), generating MORE tokens. Counterintuitive but real: on an easy-enough task, injecting precise relevant context is NET-NEGATIVE (the agent pays to process knowledge it didn't need). THE FULL PATTERN (5 versions, 5 NO-WINs, each missing a DIFFERENT necessary condition): v1 = agent didn't consult (unused); v2/v3 = task too easy → zero hardness → parity; v4 = task HARD (H~18k) but knowledge too GENERAL → couldn't collapse; v5 = knowledge PRECISE+RETRIEVED but task too EASY (H~2k) → over-engagement → ON does MORE. The conditions to WIN are conjunctive and narrow: (a) task hard enough OFF spends real hardness, AND (b) precise answer in KB, AND (c) retrievable, AND (d) agent uses it to SHORTCUT not over-deliberate. We hit (a) XOR (b+c) but never together; and (d) is its own risk (v5 shows forced retrieval backfires). IMPLICATION: retrieval should be OPT-IN/difficulty-gated, not forced (v1+v5: forcing consult on easy tasks hurts; a free agent skips it → neutral). For a strong model the net-positive regime is narrow; forcing a single-task WIN now edges toward rigging. The genuine unfalsified value is COMPOUNDING over a real workload (task N reuses task N-1..1's precise resolutions) — which a contrived single-task bench cannot fairly test. JUDGMENT: conclude the single-task benchma
